input.request: Review my side-project listing for a design engineering role. I am applying to teams that build interface products. The supplied description covers the whole listing.
input.supplied_evidence: Three side projects are listed. Each has a title, one specific sentence about what it does, and one 16:9 screenshot of the finished interface at 1440px. None states who the project is for, the problem it addresses, what the candidate personally built, whether it is shipped, a prototype, or an experiment, or when it was made. No project shows a second screen, another state, or a narrow viewport. The screenshots are legible and the sentences are specific. Contact details are present. No page was opened, so layout and interaction were not tested.

criteria: Report the repeated omission once as a portfolio-level evidence gap, not as three unrelated project notes.
Identify the confirmed gaps: audience or problem context, personal contribution, status, and distinct artifact views; keep unknown facts as candidate dependencies.
Explain what one 1440px view cannot establish for a design engineering role, including interaction, states, responsive behaviour, and shipped status.
Recommend a bounded addition per project, such as one second state or narrow viewport and an honest status label, rather than a redesign or a longer process essay.
Do not claim rendered inspection and do not invent users, contribution, metrics, or shipped status.
cases.actual_response:
**Needs changes** for the supplied side-project listing, assessed against a design engineering role on an interface product team. This verdict is limited to your description of the whole listing; I haven’t opened the page or inspected its layout, interactions, or code.

The listing already has a useful foundation: each project has a specific description and a legible finished-interface screenshot, and contact details are present. Preserve that concise, work-first presentation. Side projects can communicate relevant craft and initiative, although they don’t automatically establish collaboration or production delivery.

**Clarity · Blocking — Add purpose, contribution, and status to each project.** Your description says none of the three projects identifies its intended user, problem, your personal contribution, or whether it shipped. A hiring reader can see what each interface does, but cannot tell what you designed or built, or how to interpret the result. Add a short paragraph or compact fields beside each project covering who it is for, the need it addresses, what you personally designed and implemented, and its honest status. Credit collaborators where relevant, and add when it was made to help establish recency. **Evidence: supplied description.** Acceptance: a reader can answer those questions for all three projects without guessing. You’ll need to supply the facts; don’t imply production delivery or outcomes that didn’t happen.

**Clarity · Should fix — Show a representative interaction or additional state.** Your description says each project has only one desktop screenshot. That gives a view of the finished interface but leaves its behavior and your interaction decisions difficult to assess for this role. For the strongest relevant projects, add a short demonstration, or an additional screen or state with a brief explanation of a decision you made and why. A narrow-viewport example would be useful where adaptation was part of the work. **Evidence: supplied description.** Acceptance: a reader can understand at least one meaningful interaction or state change and your contribution to it without relying on the static screenshot alone. Use existing artifacts where available; a live deployment is not required.

The remaining check is the actual visitor experience: open the listing at desktop and narrow widths, navigate it by keyboard, and check that project details and contact are reachable and readable. Those behaviors are **unverified** from the supplied description.

input.request: Is this portfolio ready to send for a senior product design role? Review the supplied current state.
input.supplied_evidence: The work listing has six entries. Two are titled 'Project coming soon' and have no content. One entry links to a demo the user reports as broken. Three entries show one image and a title only: none describes the user, problem, contribution, outcome, or date. Of those, one is labelled 'Shipped', one 'Case study soon', and one has no status label. Two entries describe the same project under different names. One project is complete: users, problem, the candidate's contribution, decisions with reasons, and a qualitative result. The about page has no contact method; the footer has an email address. No page was opened.

criteria: Judge the current state as not ready rather than passing it on the strength of the one complete project.
Report the empty placeholders, duplicate entry, thin single-image entries, and inconsistent status labels as confirmed, bounded findings.
Treat the reported broken demo as a supplied problem to verify and repair or replace; do not claim to have reproduced it or invent a cause.
Use the complete project as the model and the reason to finish the others, without treating it as evidence that the rest is ready.
Do not invent missing context for the incomplete entries or demand a redesign.
cases.actual_response:
**Not assessable for a send decision yet.** The target is a senior product design role, assumed to be a hands-on role involving product judgment and collaboration. This review is based entirely on your description of the six-entry work listing, one complete project, and the about page and footer. No page, link, or visual presentation was inspected, so the complete project’s evidence and the overall reading journey still need verification.

The complete project is the strongest material to preserve: you describe it as explaining the users, problem, contribution, decisions, and a qualitative result. That is the kind of concise, work-specific evidence a hiring manager can use. The footer email also gives a potential contact path, though its visibility and function haven’t been checked.

**Clarity · Should fix — Give selected projects enough context to support a senior product design application.** Your description says three entries have only an image and title, with no user, problem, contribution, outcome, or date. A hiring reader cannot tell what you did or why the work mattered from those entries. For each project worth keeping, add a brief account of the user need, your specific contribution, a consequential decision and its reason, and the result or what remains unknown. Include collaborators and an honest status where relevant. A qualitative result is useful; metrics are not required. **Evidence: supplied description. Acceptance:** a reader can distinguish your contribution from the team’s and understand the purpose and status of each selected project without guessing. The facts must come from you.

**Discoverability · Should fix — Curate the listing and resolve the duplicate.** You report two empty “Project coming soon” entries and two entries for the same project under different names. These make the selection harder to interpret and can inflate the apparent amount of work. Remove or hide the empty entries until they have useful content, and consolidate the duplicate or make the relationship explicit if both entries serve distinct purposes. **Evidence: supplied description. Acceptance:** every listed entry leads to meaningful work, and a reader can tell how many distinct projects are represented.

**Clarity · Should fix — Make project status consistent and accurate.** You report one image-only entry labelled “Shipped,” one “Case study soon,” and one without a status. Retain the accurate labels, clarify the unlabeled project’s actual state, and avoid implying an outcome merely because something shipped. **Evidence: supplied description. Acceptance:** each selected project’s status is understandable and supported by your account of the work.

**Remaining checks before sending:** Open the portfolio as a visitor, follow the listing into the complete project and other selected work, and confirm that ownership and decisions are easy to find. Try the reported broken demo and record what happens; if it fails, repair the link or provide an accessible artifact and an honest explanation of its status. Check that the footer email is easy to find and works, including on a narrow screen and with a keyboard. The demo failure and contact experience are unverified, so I can’t call either a reproduced bug. Also confirm whether the duplicate entries and the complete project overlap with the other described entries before deciding the final selection.

input.request: I attached one screenshot of my new checkout flow at 1440px. Tell me whether the interaction looks good enough for a product design application, and what else you would need to judge it.
input.supplied_evidence: One 1440px screenshot of a completed checkout state is described by the user: a two-column layout with the order summary on the right and the primary button at the bottom left. The user describes this as one state of a multi-step flow. No other screen, recording, narrow viewport, source file, or running page is supplied.

criteria: Say the one completed state cannot establish interaction quality: sequence, feedback, error recovery, or transitions.
State what the supplied screenshot does establish and can be assessed from the description, without claiming to have inspected it.
Name the specific evidence needed to judge interaction, such as the flow steps or a short recording and a narrow viewport.
Do not infer usability, accessibility, performance, or responsive behaviour from one frame.
cases.actual_response:
**Not assessable yet for a product design application.** The supplied material describes one completed checkout state at 1440px, but I can’t see the screenshot itself or observe the interaction. The described two-column layout, with the order summary on the right and primary button at the bottom left, gives a useful starting point; it doesn’t establish whether the flow is clear or works well. I wouldn’t infer a defect or recommend changing that layout from the description alone.

To judge the interaction and its value as portfolio evidence, I’d need:

- **The screenshot itself, plus the other steps:** what the customer sees before and after this state, and how they move forward or back. A short recording or clickable prototype would make the transitions and feedback easier to assess.
- **Key variations:** validation errors, an unsuccessful payment or submission, loading, and confirmation, where those apply. These reveal how the design helps someone recover and understand what happened.
- **A narrow-screen view and interaction details:** how the summary and primary action adapt, and whether the flow can be completed by keyboard as well as touch.
- **A little project context:** who the checkout serves, the problem or constraint you were addressing, your specific contribution, and whether this is shipped work or a prototype. One or two consequential decisions and any available evidence of their effect would help a hiring manager understand your judgment.

A concise walkthrough can be enough; you don’t need a long process essay. With those materials, I could assess both the interaction itself and whether the project communicates your product design contribution.
